primitives.name: Ranking Lasso
primitives.verbatim_quote: This paper suggests fitting paired comparison models with a lassotype procedure that forces contestants with similar abilities to be classified into the same group.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'Y_{ijr}': 'binary outcome of match between teams i and j at round r', '\\mu_i': 'ability parameter for team i (dimensionless)', '\\tau': 'home-field advantage parameter (dimensionless)', '\\lambda': 'regularization strength (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Paired comparisons follow logistic model; contestants with similar abilities are grouped; model identified via sum-to-zero constraint on abilities.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \lambda \to 0, reduces to standard MLE; when \lambda \to \infty, all teams grouped into single class.

layer2.mapping: The lasso penalty induces a grouping structure on team abilities, aligning with GSI's need for coherent probabilistic rankings and GSE's requirement for state transition consistency in multi-agent sports environments.
layer2.telemetry: Prediction accuracy, rank stability across rounds, and group cohesion metrics.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core idea of the ranking lasso is to regularize the Bradley-Terry model using a lasso-type penalty that encourages similar team abilities to be grouped together. This is achieved by minimizing a penalized log-likelihood function where the penalty term is the sum of absolute differences between team abilities. The resulting estimator promotes sparsity in the differences, effectively clustering teams with comparable strengths. The Bradley-Terry model itself defines the probability of one team beating another based on their relative abilities, which is central to any ranking system. Its logistic form ensures bounded probabilities and tractable optimization. The grouping mechanism enhances interpretability and prediction quality by reducing overfitting and noise in the estimated abilities. The method is particularly useful in sports where teams face each other in pairwise competitions, such as football or hockey. It addresses the challenge of assigning meaningful ranks to teams when raw win-loss records may not reflect true competitive strength. The lasso penalty acts as a dual constraint to the likelihood maximization, balancing fit and simplicity. The model assumes independence of pairwise comparisons and that team abilities can be represented as scalar values. Failure modes occur when the regularization parameter is mis-specified, leading to under- or over-clustering. The approach also inherits limitations from the Bradley-Terry model, such as sensitivity to home-field effects and assumption of transitivity in preferences.
